title: Enterprise registration is not worker formalization: construction exposes the portability gap
source_unit: International Labour Organization, Informality in Nepal's Construction Sector: Promoting enterprise formalization and extending social protection to construction workers, 2026
geography: Nepal construction sector, with national labor-market, enterprise and stakeholder evidence

observations.period: 2018–2023; construction-sector employment, enterprise and informality indicators

denominator.unit: Nepal construction-sector labor and enterprise frame

sector_weight.value: >6% of GDP and approximately 14% of national employment

informality.unit: percent informal employment in construction in 2023

registered_unit_gap.unit: percent of workers in formally registered construction enterprises who were informal in 2018

precarity.value: 99.8% of informal construction jobs were temporary in 2018 and 81.9% of informal workers were paid daily

distribution.value: 35.6% of construction workers were below the minimum wage and construction-worker poverty was 27.4% in 2023, versus 25.3% and 20% nationally

mechanism.value: enterprise registration can coexist with informal employment when project work, daily pay and subcontracting keep the employment relationship outside durable protection

observations.method: ILO diagnostic brief combining labor-force and enterprise statistics, stakeholder perspectives, legal and policy review, and sector-level evidence from Nepal.
observations.uncertainty: Indicators refer to different years, denominators and statistical frames; the brief is diagnostic and does not estimate a causal effect of any single formalization policy.
observations.subgroup: Daily-paid, temporary and subcontracted construction workers; workers in small firms; workers in poverty or below minimum wage; and workers whose enterprise is registered but whose employment is not formalized.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some temporary work may reflect project-based production rather than unlawful employment, and registration may still provide partial benefits even when worker-level formalization is incomplete; the figures do not by themselves identify employer intent or enforcement failure.

denominator.unit: Nepal construction worker and enterprise-owner frame

gender_presence.value: women were 10.5% of the construction workforce and 5.1% of enterprise owners

gender_pay.value: female building laborers averaged NPR 13,946 versus NPR 16,780 for men, approximately a 17% gap

gender_floor.unit: percent of women construction workers below the minimum wage

skills.unit: percent of construction employees with vocational training

risk.value: informal workers face weak occupational safety and health protection and limited injury insurance, with women concentrated in lower-paid work

mechanism.value: formalization is also a status-and-capability bargain: skills certification, wage floors, safety protection and gender equity determine whether sector growth becomes decent work

observations.method: ILO sector diagnostic using reported labor-market indicators, stakeholder evidence and policy analysis of skills, wage, gender and occupational-safety conditions.
observations.uncertainty: Gender, training and earnings indicators may be affected by occupational sorting, seasonality, reporting quality and differences in worker or firm composition; the brief does not identify causal wage or training returns.
observations.subgroup: Women workers, building laborers, workers without vocational certification, workers exposed to construction hazards, and workers excluded from injury or social-security protection.
observations.counterinterpretation: Training alone may not raise earnings where subcontracting and weak enforcement persist; measured gender gaps may partly reflect job type, tenure or hours rather than unequal pay for identical work.

observations.period: 2026 policy diagnosis; temporary, mobile and subcontracted work as a social-protection design problem

denominator.unit: Nepal construction formalization and social-protection policy frame

barrier.value: frequent employer and worksite changes, irregular earnings, layered subcontracting, missing employer-of-record clarity, weak inspection and barriers involving citizenship certificates, bank accounts and digital literacy

procurement.value: public procurement is identified as a leverage point, while rules allowing up to 25% subcontracting do not clearly require formalization of subcontracted workers

adaptation.value: the brief recommends simplified or single-window enrollment, flexible contributions, portable benefits, worker-initiated enrollment, government co-contributions, awareness, foreign-worker access and stronger coordination

mechanism.value: when work, residence, employer and payment channels move faster than the social-security account, formalization requires portability and continuity infrastructure rather than enterprise registration alone

observations.method: ILO policy diagnostic drawing on stakeholder consultations, legal and institutional review, sector statistics and recommendations for procurement, inspection, skills, social protection and gender-responsive implementation.
observations.uncertainty: Recommendations are a policy agenda rather than tested interventions; the brief does not establish which mix of portability, subsidies, enforcement or digital integration would produce durable registration or better outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Mobile and seasonal workers, subcontracted workers, foreign workers, women in low-paid roles, small contractors, workers lacking identity or banking access, and public agencies responsible for procurement and social protection.
observations.counterinterpretation: Simplifying enrollment or making benefits portable may not overcome contribution affordability, low trust or weak benefit delivery; stronger procurement conditions could also raise costs or exclude small contractors unless paired with finance and technical support.

related_sources.claim: Official ILO publication page with the brief, date, DOI and summary of construction informality and formalization findings.
Official DOI for the Nepal construction-sector brief.

boundary: This record identifies construction as a high-informality social-protection and portability problem: enterprise registration, worker formalization, safety, skills, gender equity and procurement are coupled but distinct. It is a diagnostic policy brief, not causal evidence that any individual recommendation improves registration, earnings, safety, poverty, gender equity or social trust.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ILO eight-page PDF and publication page, sector weight, informality, temporary and daily-paid work, poverty and minimum-wage contrasts, gender and skills indicators, subcontracting and procurement issues, identity and digital barriers, and portability-oriented recommendations were reviewed.
